title: Compensation Adjustment Notice
topic: A raise that does not actually undo a cut
blurb: HR sent the adjusted offer and said last year's change is now behind you.
prompt: You asked an AI to summarize this HR memo. If a line doesn't add up, tap it.

segments.label: The old salary
segments.text: Before last year's downturn, your base salary was $100,000.

segments.label: Last year's change
segments.text: During the downturn, the company reduced your salary by 20%, to $80,000.

segments.label: This year's letter
segments.text: This year's letter grants a 20% raise, calculated on your current salary.

segments.label: HR's reading
segments.text: Because the percentage reduction and the percentage raise are the same size, the new salary returns you to $100,000.

segments.label: Next step
segments.text: HR recommends signing this week so the adjustment can take effect next month.

conclusion: AI summary: the raise matches last year's reduction, so the new salary is $100,000 again. Signing is fine.

flaws.original: The 20% raise is applied to the reduced $80,000 salary ($80,000 × 1.20 = $96,000), so you are still $4,000 short of $100,000.
flaws.corrupted: Because the percentage reduction and the percentage raise are the same size, the new salary returns you to $100,000.

diagnosis_choices.label: 20% of $80,000 is only $16,000, so the new salary is $96,000 — still $4,000 short of $100,000.
20% of $80,000 is $18,000, which brings the salary to $98,000 — $2,000 short of $100,000.
A 20% cut followed by a 20% raise returns you to $100,000, it just ignores a year of inflation.
Because the raise applies to $80,000, it actually pushes the new salary past $100,000 to $104,000.

fix_choices.label: You need a 25% raise on $80,000 ($20,000) to get back to $100,000; 20% only reaches $96,000.
Add a 22% raise on $80,000 ($17,600) to get back to $100,000 cleanly.
Keep the 20% raise and add a 4% inflation bonus on top of $100,000.
Calculate the 20% raise on $96,000 instead of $80,000 so it hits $100,000.

flaws.explanation: A 20% cut and a 20% raise don't cancel. $100,000 falls to $80,000; 20% of $80,000 is only $16,000, so you land at $96,000. You need a 25% raise to get back.
flaws.why_tempting: Saying '−20% + 20% = 0' feels obviously right, because we treat percentages like dollar amounts.
flaws.catch_rule: Never add sequential percentage changes; multiply the factors (0.80 × 1.20 = 0.96).
flaws.hint: What's your actual salary after the cut? Now take 20% of that new number, not of $100,000.

practice.problem: A stock dropped 50% this month. What gain do you need next month just to get back to even?
practice.answer: A 100% gain — it has to double from the bottom.

clean_segments: Before last year's downturn, your base salary was $100,000.
During the downturn, the company reduced your salary by 20%, to $80,000.
This year's letter grants a 20% raise, calculated on your current salary.
After the raise, the new salary is $80,000 × 1.20 = $96,000, which is still $4,000 short of $100,000. A 25% raise would be needed to restore the original pay.
Whether you sign depends on the rest of the offer; this raise alone does not put you back to even.
clean_conclusion: The matching percentages do not cancel: the new salary is $96,000, not $100,000.

diagnosis: $100,000 base salary leaves out bonuses and equity, so percentage changes on base don't tell the full story.
A $100,000 base from last year is already worth less after inflation, even if it returned to $100,000.
You can't compare a $100,000 pre-downturn salary against post-downturn pay without adjusting tax brackets.
Calling $100,000 the baseline hides that a 20% cut only lowered take-home pay by ~15% after tax.
fix: Include annual bonus and stock grants alongside the $100,000 base.
Index the $100,000 baseline for inflation (~$103,000) before comparing.
Compare after-tax net pay instead of gross $100,000.
Verify whether $100,000 was annualized before or after last year's merit cycle.

diagnosis: Reducing $100,000 by 20% removes $20,000, which means a 20% raise later adds back the same $20,000.
Cutting $100,000 to $80,000 is a 25% reduction, not a 20% reduction.
Saying 'during the downturn' doesn't specify how many months you were paid at $80,000.
fix: Label the drop from $100,000 to $80,000 as a 25% cut.
Count the lost $20,000 from last year as back pay owed on top of the raise.
Verify the exact effective date of the cut to $80,000.

diagnosis: Calculating the 20% raise on your current $80,000 salary is standard, so it automatically restores $20,000.
Saying '20% raise on your current salary' contradicts HR policy, which calculates raises off the original $100,000.
20% on $80,000 is $16,000 — that's 16% of $100,000, which is fine as long as the letter doesn't claim $100,000.
A 20% raise in one year pushes you into a higher tax bracket that wipes out the $16,000.
fix: Ask HR to calculate the 20% raise on the pre-cut $100,000 base instead of $80,000.
State the dollar amount ($16,000 raise to $96,000) right inside line 3.
Request a 25% raise on $80,000 so the new salary actually returns to $100,000.
Split the 20% raise across two 10% bumps so taxes don't jump.

diagnosis: Signing this week locks you into $96,000 instead of $100,000 before you can point out the $4,000 gap.
Waiting until next month loses another month at $80,000, which costs more than the $4,000 gap.
HR pushing for a signature this week proves the $100,000 figure was a deliberate typo.
Even if you sign this week, the raise doesn't back-pay the $20,000 cut from last year.
fix: Ask HR to fix the letter to $100,000 (25% on $80,000) before signing.
Sign immediately to start getting $96,000 next month, then negotiate the last $4,000 later.
Request retroactive back pay for last year's cut before signing.
Ask HR to put the exact new dollar salary in writing on the signature line.
